summary: This RFC reproduces the then-current text of the ISO Transport Protocol, a Draft International Standard being voted on in ISO. It is only for information and does not specify a standard for the ARPA Internet. It replaced RFC 892.

eli5.summary: This is a copy of another organization's draft rulebook for moving data between computers, shared so people could read and compare it.

questions: what are the iso transport protocol classes
subtitle: A retyped ISO draft standard for the transport layer, with five protocol classes for networks of very different quality.

tldr.problem: Networks differ widely in how often they lose, corrupt or reset connections, so one transport protocol with one set of behaviours cannot serve them all at a sensible cost.
tldr.mechanism: The draft defines five classes (0 to 4) built from shared elements of procedure, a negotiation in the CR and CC messages to pick a class and options, and one common encoding for all transport protocol data units.
tldr.outcome: This RFC only reproduces the then-current ISO Draft International Standard text, for information. It does not specify a standard for the ARPA-Internet, and it supersedes RFC 892.

today: RFC 905 was distributed for information only and never specified a standard for the ARPA-Internet. It states that it supersedes RFC 892, an older version of the same ISO text, and no later RFC is recorded as replacing it.

sections.title: What This Document Is
sections.content:
RFC 905 is a retyped copy of ISO DP 8073, the ISO Transport Protocol Specification. The memo says it was prepared by retyping ISO/TC97/SC16/N1576 and applying the proposed editorial corrections in ISO/TC97/SC16/N1695. Together these two documents were being voted on within ISO as a Draft International Standard.

The status note is plain: the document is distributed for information only and does not specify a standard for the ARPA-Internet. The memo also warns that typographic errors not present in the ISO documents may have been overlooked. Its note 1 says RFC 892 is an older version of the specification, so this RFC should be assumed to supersede RFC 892.
sections.eli5: Someone retyped another club's draft rulebook so everyone could read it. They said it is just for reading, and it replaces an older copy.

sections.title: Scope and Place in the OSI Stack
sections.content:
The standard sits between two other ISO drafts. It supports the transport service defined in DP 8072 and assumes the connection-oriented network service defined in DP 8348. It is positioned by the layers of the OSI Reference Model (ISO 7498).

It specifies five classes of procedures for the connection-oriented transfer of data and control information between peer transport entities, the means of negotiating the class, and the structure and encoding of the protocol data units. Procedures are described through three kinds of interaction: exchanges of TPDUs between peers, transport service primitives with the user, and network service primitives with the network provider.

The introduction is candid about limits. It does not define how to measure quality of service or when to release a connection after quality degrades. It also notes that, because the number of valid protocol sequences is very large, an implementation cannot be fully verified by testing.
sections.eli5: The rulebook says where it fits: it uses the roads below it and serves the programs above it. It tells the two ends how to talk, but not how to judge whether the road is any good.

sections.title: Five Classes for Three Kinds of Network
sections.content:
The functions of the transport layer are organized into classes and options. A class defines a set of functions; options define which functions within a class may or may not be used. The classes are meant to match the quality of the network connection, which the text sorts into three types:

  • Type A: acceptable residual error rate and acceptable rate of signalled errors.
  • Type B: acceptable residual error rate but an unacceptable rate of signalled errors.
  • Type C: unacceptable residual error rate.

Class 0 (Simple) is designed for type A and is fully compatible with CCITT recommendation S.70 for teletex terminals. Class 1 (Basic error recovery) mainly recovers from network disconnect or reset and is designed for type B. Class 2 (Multiplexing) shares one network connection among several transport connections and is designed for type A. Class 3 adds Class 1 style recovery to multiplexing, for type B. Class 4 (Error detection and recovery) adds detection and recovery of TPDU loss, misordering, duplication and corruption, for type C.
sections.eli5: There are five versions of the rules. Smooth roads need only a simple version. Roads where packages get lost or scrambled need a version with extra checking and re-sending.

sections.title: Connection Setup, Refusal and Release
sections.content:
A transport connection starts when the initiator sends a Connection Request (CR) TPDU and the responder answers with a Connection Confirm (CC) TPDU. Each side picks a 16-bit reference for the peer to use; it must not be zero and must not be in use or frozen. User data in a CR is not allowed in Class 0 and is limited to 32 octets in the other classes.

If the responder cannot accept, it replies with a Disconnect Request (DR) whose source reference is zero. An invalid CR can be answered with an Error (ER) or DR TPDU.

Release has two variants. Class 0 uses an implicit release: disconnecting the network connection ends the transport connection. Classes 1 to 4 use an explicit release with a DR answered by a Disconnect Confirm (DC), so a transport connection can end independently of the network connection.
sections.eli5: To start, one side says 'can we talk?' and the other says 'yes, here is my number.' To finish, one says 'goodbye' and the other says 'goodbye received.' The simplest version just hangs up the phone.

sections.title: Negotiating Class and Options
sections.content:
The initiator proposes a preferred class and may list alternative classes in the CR. The responder must select one class that Table 3 of the RFC allows as a valid response and report it in the CC. Negotiating from Class 2 to Class 1, or from any class to a higher-numbered class, is not valid. If class 3 or 4 is proposed, class 2 is an implicit valid response, and if class 1 is proposed, class 0 is.

Other things are negotiated too. The initiator proposes a maximum TPDU size and the responder may accept it or answer with any value between 128 and the proposed value. The CR itself does not exceed 128 octets. Options such as extended format (classes 2, 3, 4), non-use of explicit flow control (Class 2 only), non-use of checksum (Class 4 only) and the transport expedited data service follow a simple rule: the initiator proposes yes or no, and the responder may accept a yes or choose no, but must follow a no.

Quality of service parameters (throughput, residual error rate, priority and transit delay) are also carried in the CR and CC. Transit delay values are based on a TSDU size of 128 octets.
sections.eli5: It is like agreeing on rules before a game. One side says which version it wants and which backups it would accept, and the other picks one that is allowed. Nobody can pick a fancier version than was offered.

sections.title: Moving Data: Numbering, Windows and Recovery
sections.content:
A user message (TSDU) is mapped onto one or more Data (DT) TPDUs, with an end-of-TSDU mark showing whether more follow. TPDUs can be concatenated into one network message in classes 1 to 4, and the last one in a concatenated set carries the data.

Where the class needs it, DT TPDUs are numbered starting from zero, using modulo 27 arithmetic in the normal format and modulo 231 in the extended format. Classes 2, 3 and 4 use explicit flow control with a credit (CDT), and acknowledgements are carried in AK TPDUs.

Expedited data bypasses normal flow control. Each ED TPDU is acknowledged by an EA TPDU, only one ED TPDU may be unacknowledged per direction, and a zero-length ED TPDU is a protocol error.

For recovery, classes 1 and 3 can reassign a connection to a new network connection after a signalled disconnect and then resynchronize, using the timers TTR (time to try) and TWR (time to wait). Copies of CR, CC, DR, DT and ED TPDUs are retained until acknowledged.
sections.eli5: Big messages are cut into numbered pieces so the other side can put them back in order and say which ones arrived. If the road breaks, the sender picks a new road and asks where to carry on from.

sections.title: Class 4 Timers, Checksums and Frozen References
sections.content:
Class 4 assumes the network may lose, duplicate, reorder or corrupt TPDUs without telling anyone. It adds retransmission on time-out: if no acknowledgement arrives within T1, the TPDU is resent, and after N transmissions the connection is released and the user is informed. An inactivity timer I starts release if no TPDU arrives at all, and receivers resequence out-of-order TPDUs. The RFC deliberately gives no fixed values for these timers; they should be chosen to suit the known network.

The checksum is used only in Class 4. It is always present in the CR and is used on other TPDUs unless non-use was agreed. It is a 16-bit parameter chosen so that two sums over the octets are zero modulo 255. The RFC admits it will not detect insertion or loss of leading or trailing zeros, nor some octet misordering.

A frozen reference is a connection reference held out of use after release so that old delayed TPDUs cannot be mistaken for a new connection. It is never required in classes 0 and 2, is used in classes 1 and 3 with exceptions, and is always used in Class 4, for longer than L.
sections.eli5: On a bumpy road, the sender keeps a copy, sets a timer, and sends again if no thank-you comes back. Old ticket numbers are put on a shelf for a while so nobody confuses them with new ones.

sections.title: Structure and Encoding of TPDUs
sections.content:
Every TPDU has a header and an optional data field. The header is a length indicator (LI) octet, a fixed part and an optional variable part. LI has a maximum value of 254, counts the header excluding the LI octet and the user data, and the value 255 is reserved for extensions. The TPDU code is in octet 2. For CR, CC, RJ and AK the high four bits are the code and the low four bits carry the credit.

The variable part is a series of parameters, each with a code, a length and a value, in any order. A later duplicate wins. An undefined parameter is ignored in a CR but is a protocol error in other TPDUs.

Parameters defined in the CR include calling and called TSAP identifiers, TPDU size (from 128 up to 8192 octets, with 4096 and 8192 not allowed in Class 0), version number, security parameters, checksum, additional option selection, alternative classes, acknowledge time, throughput, residual error rate, priority, transit delay and the reassignment (TTR) time in seconds.
sections.eli5: Every message starts with a label saying how long the label is, what kind of message it is, and then optional extra stickers. The receiver reads the label first to know how to handle the rest.

sections.title: Conformance Rules
sections.content:
Clause 14 sets minimum rules for a system that claims to implement the standard. It must implement Class 0 or Class 2 or both. If it implements Class 3 or Class 4 it must also implement Class 2, and if it implements Class 1 it must also implement Class 0.

For each class claimed, the system must be able to initiate CR TPDUs or respond with CC TPDUs, or both, and must handle all TPDUs up to the smaller of the class maximum and the maximum claimed. TPDU sizes of 128 octets are always implemented. A conformance claim must state the classes, whether the system initiates, responds or both, which optional procedures it implements, and its maximum TPDU size.

The standard contains no tests to demonstrate conformance. Annex A (state tables) and Annex B (checksum algorithms) are part of the document; in this copy the state tables are omitted, and the text takes precedence over the tables if they differ.
sections.eli5: If a maker says its product follows the rulebook, it must support at least the basic version and must say exactly which versions and extras it supports. The rulebook gives no exam to check the claim.
